## What we found

- **Paid doctors' GLP-1 prescribing tilts a few points toward the paying brand.** Compared with similar doctors not yet paid, the paid brand's share of their GLP-1 claims rises by {{< var share_trulicity >}} percentage points for Trulicity, {{< var share_ozempic >}} for Ozempic and {{< var share_mounjaro >}} for Mounjaro, mostly at the expense of direct competitors. The direction holds in every version we ran; the size does not. If the brand rows Medicare hides (0 to 10 claims) are bounded against the result, the gains shrink to {{< var bound_trulicity >}} / {{< var bound_ozempic >}} / {{< var bound_mounjaro >}}, and in the pre-registered model only Mounjaro's gain is clearly above zero. Victoza's share falls.
- **Paid doctors' practices were already growing.** They become more likely to have 11 or more claims of the paid brand in a year ({{< var att_trulicity >}} / {{< var att_victoza >}} / {{< var att_ozempic >}} percentage points for Trulicity, Victoza and Ozempic), but their statin prescribing, which a GLP-1 payment has no direct reason to change, rises too ({{< var statin_trulicity >}} / {{< var statin_victoza >}} / {{< var statin_ozempic >}}).
- **The money is concentrated.** From 2013 to 2025, drug makers paid ${{< var promo_usd_m >}} million in promotional payments naming a GLP-1 (including ${{< var obesity_usd_m >}} million naming the obesity drugs Wegovy, Saxenda and Zepbound) to about {{< var paid_npis_k >}},000 prescribers. Through 2024, the top 1% of paid prescribers received {{< var top1_share >}}% of the dollars, {{< var top1_speaker_share >}}% of that as speaker fees; the median paid prescriber received ${{< var median_usd >}} over twelve years.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## What this doesn't mean

- **It does not show that payments caused prescribing.** Companies choose whom to pay, and representatives call when a brand has news: Ozempic and Trulicity both gained cardiovascular indications in early 2020, and shortages in 2022–2024 forced switches. The share shift is *consistent with* payments influencing brand choice, but it could also reflect paid doctors adopting newly launched brands sooner.
- **It is not a precise effect size.** The share gain is somewhere between about {{< var bound_range >}} and {{< var share_range >}} points depending on choices the data cannot settle.
- **It is not evidence of inappropriate prescribing.** GLP-1s are effective diabetes drugs, several with proven cardiovascular benefit, and the brands are not interchangeable: they differ in dosing frequency, potency and evidence. Much of the switching runs in the direction guidelines favoured at the time.
- **It says nothing about obesity prescribing or about any individual doctor.** Part D cannot cover weight-loss-only prescriptions. Speaker and consulting fees pay for services, and concentration does not by itself imply wrongdoing. No prescriber is named, mapped or ranked anywhere in this project.
:::

## The question

Between 2013 and 2024, Medicare Part D gross spending on GLP-1 drugs (before manufacturer rebates) grew from ${{< var spend_2013 >}} billion to ${{< var spend_2024 >}} billion a year. Over the same years the companies that make them, chiefly Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, paid doctors for meals, talks, consulting and travel, and the federal Open Payments program published every payment.

Two decades of research find that doctors who take industry money prescribe more of the payer's drugs [@dejong2016; @yeh2016; @fleischman2016; @hadland2018; @mitchell2021]. Almost all of that work compares paid and unpaid doctors at one point in time, so it cannot tell influence from targeting: drug representatives visit the doctors who already prescribe, or are about to prescribe, the most. The one GLP-1 study so far is also a cross-sectional snapshot [@khunte2026].

This project asks a narrower, harder question: **when a doctor receives a first promotional payment for a specific GLP-1 brand, does their prescribing of *that brand* change afterwards, compared with similar doctors who have not yet been paid — and does it change in ways that targeting alone would not produce?**

## The data

Everything here comes from public federal data.

- **CMS Open Payments**, the "Sunshine Act" database: {{< var glp1_records_m >}} million general payments that name a GLP-1 brand, 2013–2025. We keep the promotional ones (meals, speaker and consulting fees, travel, education, gifts) and drop royalties, research grants and acquisitions. A payment naming several drugs is split equally between them for dollar totals. Ozempic and Rybelsus are often promoted together, so "Ozempic" exposure largely means semaglutide promotion; counting any semaglutide brand as exposure gives a similar result ({{< var molecule_ozempic >}} points on the 11-claims outcome).
- **Medicare Part D Prescribers by Provider and Drug**, 2013–2024: each prescriber's yearly claims (pharmacy fills) for each drug, linked to Open Payments by National Provider Identifier. The link is near-complete: {{< var link_2013 >}}% of physician payment records in 2013 and at least {{< var link_2015 >}}% from 2015 on.
- **The analysis panel** follows {{< var n_diabetes >}} prescribers who treat diabetes regularly (out of {{< var n_partd_prescribers >}} Part D prescribers), each GLP-1 brand and each year. The main event study uses the {{< var n_physicians >}} physicians among them, because payments to nurse practitioners and physician assistants were not reported before 2021.

Two features of the data shape every result:

1. **Medicare hides small counts.** A prescriber-drug row with fewer than 11 claims in a year is suppressed. A missing row means "0 to 10 claims", not zero. The main outcome is therefore *whether* a doctor had at least 11 claims of the brand that year (roughly one patient refilling monthly, or a few on longer supplies), which is always observed; prescription volumes are estimated separately with bounds for the hidden cells.
2. **Most GLP-1 prescribing comes from doctors who are paid at some point.** {{< var fills_paid_2013 >}}% of GLP-1 fills in 2013, and {{< var fills_paid_2024 >}}% in 2024, came from prescribers who received a GLP-1 payment in some year. So the comparison group is mostly doctors **not paid yet**, not doctors never paid.

## How we measured it, in plain English

**Before looking at any result, we wrote down the analysis and locked it.** The pre-registration ([PREREGISTRATION.md](https://github.com/johnpospisil/pharma-payments-glp1/blob/main/PREREGISTRATION.md)) fixed the outcome, the comparison, the estimator, the tests that could prove the finding wrong, and how each pattern of results would be described. Every later change is logged there as a dated deviation, and two matter for how you read this article. The pre-registered primary outcome (at least 11 claims) failed its own falsification tests; brand share was a pre-registered *secondary* question, and we chose to lead with it after seeing those failures. We also changed the implementation of the primary estimator after the first results; the first-reported estimates were {{< var first_trulicity >}} / {{< var first_victoza >}} / {{< var first_ozempic >}} points.

**The comparison.** For each brand, doctors enter the study in the year of their first promotional payment for it. Each one is compared with doctors in the same years who had not yet been paid for that brand, and who had a similar diabetes workload, overall Medicare volume, prior GLP-1 prescribing, specialty and region. The estimator, from @callaway2021 with the doubly robust adjustment of @santanna2020, is built for exactly this staggered timing; simpler two-way fixed-effects regressions can give badly wrong answers when timing varies [@goodmanbacon2021; @roth2023]. All differences are in percentage points (pp): a share rising from one fifth to one quarter of a doctor's claims is a 5-point rise.

**The tests that could sink it.** If payments simply mark doctors who were already on the way up, three things should show:

- **a rising trend *before* the first payment** (checked with pre-period estimates and the sensitivity bounds of @rambachan2023);
- **the same "effect" on drugs the payment has nothing to do with**, here statins (a *negative-control outcome*, @lipsitch2010);
- **an effect that disappears when paid doctors are matched to unpaid doctors with the same prior trajectory** [coarsened exact matching, @iacus2012].

**Brand share.** The second line of evidence asks how the paid brand's *share* of the doctor's own GLP-1 prescribing changes. A doctor whose practice is simply growing should prescribe more of every brand, so share largely removes practice size, in the spirit of @dejong2016. It does not remove a tendency to adopt newly launched brands sooner, and it is measured on the claims Medicare shows, which matters (Result 1).

**Who this describes.** Nearly all newly paid doctors were first reached through sponsored meals: {{< var share_under_100 >}}% received under $100 in their first payment year. The {{< var glp1_speakers >}} doctors ever paid as GLP-1 speakers were mostly first paid before 2015, so they are outside the event study. The estimate covers entering a paid relationship with a manufacturer, usually starting with a lunch, including any later payments and visits; it does not describe speakers.

## Result 1: the paid brand gains a few points of share

Among doctors who already prescribe GLP-1s (@fig-hero, top of page), the paid brand's share of their GLP-1 claims rises after the first payment for one to two years and then levels off. Averaged over the payment year and the three years after, the gain is **{{< var share_trulicity >}} percentage points for Trulicity, {{< var share_ozempic >}} for Ozempic and {{< var share_mounjaro >}} for Mounjaro** (measured from its 2022 launch, so its cohorts have at most two years of follow-up).

**How much of it is real depends on Medicare's hidden counts.** The share is computed from the brand rows Medicare shows. A paid brand that grows from, say, 8 claims (hidden, counted as zero) to 12 (shown) appears to jump from no share to a positive one, and crossing the 11-claim line is exactly what growing practices do (Result 2). Bounding the hidden rows against the result (the paid brand's hidden rows at their maximum, competitors' at zero) shrinks the gains to {{< var bound_trulicity >}} / {{< var bound_ozempic >}} / {{< var bound_mounjaro >}} points. That is still above zero, but below the 2-point threshold the pre-registration set as the smallest effect of interest. Two other checks leave the measured gains intact: counting 30-day fills instead of claims ({{< var fills_trulicity >}} / {{< var fills_ozempic >}} / {{< var fills_mounjaro >}}), and restricting to high-volume physicians, whose rows are rarely hidden ({{< var hv_trulicity >}} / {{< var hv_ozempic >}} / {{< var hv_mounjaro >}}).

**The pre-payment trends are mixed.** For Trulicity, the paid and comparison doctors' shares moved together beforehand (p = {{< var share_pre_trulicity >}}), but the matched version rejects parallel trends (p = {{< var share_pre_trulicity_matched >}}). Ozempic drifted upward before payment (p = {{< var share_pre_ozempic >}}), which matching removes. Mounjaro's pre-trend test (p = {{< var share_pre_mounjaro >}}) rests on about one year around its launch, so it says little. Victoza's share was already falling steeply (p {{< var share_pre_victoza_fmt >}}).

**The gain comes from direct competitors.** After a Trulicity payment, Victoza's share falls by {{< var src_tru_vic >}} points; after an Ozempic payment, Trulicity's falls by {{< var src_oz_tru >}}; after a Mounjaro payment, Lilly's own Trulicity falls by {{< var src_mj_tru >}} (with a different adjustment, Ozempic loses more). For the established brands, {{< var switch_frac_trulicity >}}% (Trulicity) and {{< var switch_frac_ozempic >}}% (Ozempic) of the extra claims after payment come from switching between brands rather than from more GLP-1 prescribing overall. Switching from daily Victoza to weekly drugs, and toward more potent ones, is also what the evidence and guidelines of the time favoured.

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart5_share_dumbbells.png){.light-content .d-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart5_share_dumbbells >}}"}
![](figures/social/chart5_share_dumbbells_1200x675.png){.light-content .m-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart5_share_dumbbells >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart5_share_dumbbells_dark.png){.dark-content .d-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart5_share_dumbbells >}}"}
![](figures/social/chart5_share_dumbbells_1200x675_dark.png){.dark-content .m-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart5_share_dumbbells >}}"}
:::

**Victoza is the exception.** Its share *falls* after a Victoza payment ({{< var share_victoza >}} points). One possible reason, not tested: Victoza payments came as once-weekly drugs (Trulicity, then Novo Nordisk's own Ozempic) displaced daily Victoza, and paid doctors started with a very high Victoza share that had room only to fall. Either way it cuts against a simple "payment wins share" reading.

::: {.doesnt-box}
**How solid is this?** The direction holds in every version we ran. The size does not. The method we committed to in advance models the share on a log-odds scale and gives similar numbers ({{< var frac_trulicity >}}, {{< var frac_ozempic >}}, {{< var frac_mounjaro >}}) but with wide margins of error: only Mounjaro is clearly above zero on its own. Combined across brands it is {{< var h5 >}} points (Holm-adjusted p = {{< var h5_holm >}}), and that combined result depends on comparing against closely matched doctors; without matching it is close to zero. Add the suppression bound above, and the honest summary is a modest, model-dependent shift of roughly {{< var bound_range >}} to {{< var share_range >}} points.
:::

## Result 2: the volume increase reflects, at least partly, who gets paid

The obvious headline would be that paid doctors become far more likely to prescribe the brand. They do: the probability of having at least 11 claims of the paid brand in a year rises by **{{< var att_trulicity >}} points for Trulicity, {{< var att_victoza >}} for Victoza and {{< var att_ozempic >}} for Ozempic** over the four years from the first payment, and matching on prior prescribing barely changes that ({{< var matched_trulicity >}} / {{< var matched_victoza >}} / {{< var matched_ozempic >}}).

But the pre-registered tests say this number cannot be read as the effect of a payment:

::: {#fig-statins .column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart1b_targeting_statins.png){.light-content .d-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart1b_targeting_statins >}}"}
![](figures/social/chart1b_targeting_statins_1200x675.png){.light-content .m-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart1b_targeting_statins >}}"}

![](figures/final/chart1b_targeting_statins_dark.png){.dark-content .d-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart1b_targeting_statins >}}"}
![](figures/social/chart1b_targeting_statins_1200x675_dark.png){.dark-content .m-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart1b_targeting_statins >}}"}

The paid brand and statins around the first payment. Data: [falsification.json](qa/falsification.json).
:::

- **Paid doctors were already rising before they were paid.** The pre-payment trend is steep and statistically clear for all three brands. If that trend had simply continued, the brand increase would be about half as large ({{< var trend_adj_trulicity >}} / {{< var trend_adj_victoza >}} / {{< var trend_adj_ozempic >}} points), close to the statin rise below.
- **Their statin prescribing rises too**: by {{< var statin_trulicity >}}, {{< var statin_victoza >}} and {{< var statin_ozempic >}} points, with an even steeper rise beforehand. A GLP-1 payment has no direct reason to change statin prescribing (though GLP-1 promotion does stress cardiovascular risk, which could spill over); a growing practice does. Paid doctors' total Medicare Part D claims grew {{< var total_claims_growth >}}% more than their comparison doctors', and {{< var matched_claims_growth >}}% more than matched comparison doctors'.
- **Matching does not remove it.** Matching on prior brand prescribing balances those variables, but not total practice growth. Matching on practice growth as well leaves the estimates almost unchanged ({{< var dev8_trulicity >}} / {{< var dev8_victoza >}} / {{< var dev8_ozempic >}}), and the statin test still fails under it.

Under the pre-registered interpretation rules, this pattern is reported as **"explained at least partly by targeting of already-rising prescribers."**

## Result 3: bigger payments, bigger changes, different doctors

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart2_dose.png){.light-content .d-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart2_dose >}}"}
![](figures/social/chart2_dose_1200x675.png){.light-content .m-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart2_dose >}}"}
![](figures/final/chart2_dose_dark.png){.dark-content .d-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart2_dose >}}"}
![](figures/social/chart2_dose_1200x675_dark.png){.dark-content .m-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart2_dose >}}"}
:::

Doctors who received $100 or more for the brand in their first payment year rose more than those who received less: {{< var dose_ge100_trulicity >}} vs {{< var dose_lt100_trulicity >}} points for Trulicity, {{< var dose_ge100_ozempic >}} vs {{< var dose_lt100_ozempic >}} for Ozempic. Doctors with four or more contacts in that year rose about twice as much as doctors with one ({{< var contacts4_trulicity >}} vs {{< var contacts1_trulicity >}}; {{< var contacts4_ozempic >}} vs {{< var contacts1_ozempic >}}). Pooled, the $100 gap is {{< var h4 >}} points.

**This is a gradient, not a dose-response.** Companies give more to doctors they expect more from, so the higher-paid groups differ in ways the comparison cannot fully remove.

**Speaker fees vs meals.** Doctors first paid with a speaker or consulting fee rose {{< var h2 >}} points more than meal-only doctors, but there are only {{< var n_fee_first >}} such doctors per brand, and the difference is not statistically clear after adjustment for multiple tests (Holm p = {{< var h2_holm >}}). The study cannot say whether speaker fees matter more than meals.

## Where the money goes

::: {.column-page-right}
![](figures/final/chart7_lorenz.png){.light-content .d-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart7_lorenz >}}"}
![](figures/social/chart7_lorenz_1200x675.png){.light-content .m-only fig-alt="{{< var alt_chart7_lorenz >}}"}

:::

GLP-1 promotional money is extremely concentrated. Of {{< var n_paid_lorenz >}} prescribers paid for a GLP-1 from 2013 to 2024 (${{< var promo_2024_m >}} million in all), the top 1% received {{< var top1_share >}}% of the dollars and the top 10% received {{< var top10_share >}}% (Gini {{< var gini >}}); the median paid prescriber received ${{< var median_usd >}} over twelve years. Speaker and consulting fees are {{< var fees_share >}}% of all GLP-1 promotional dollars, paid to {{< var glp1_speakers >}} speakers in all; meals are {{< var meal_share >}}%. These totals include payments naming the obesity drugs Wegovy, Saxenda and Zepbound ({{< var obesity_pct >}}% of the dollars).

Per Medicare Part D enrollee with diabetes, GLP-1 promotional payments in 2024 ranged from ${{< var state_min >}} to ${{< var state_max >}} across the states shown, against ${{< var state_us >}} nationally. Because the money is so concentrated, state values largely reflect where a small number of speakers practise, not what a typical doctor there receives. {{< var masked_states >}} are withheld to protect privacy. To look up payments and prescribing for one specialty and state, brand by brand, use the [companion explorer](app/).

Relative to diabetes workload, endocrinologists receive about {{< var endo_ratio >}} times as much per claim as primary-care physicians (${{< var endo_per_1000 >}} vs ${{< var pc_per_1000 >}} per 1,000 other diabetes-drug claims in 2024), consistent with speakers being concentrated among specialists.

## Who responds

The pre-registered secondary questions, each adjusted together for multiple testing [@holm1979]:

::: {.table-scroll}
| Question | Estimate | Holm-adjusted p | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Speaker or consulting fee vs meals only | {{< var h2 >}} pp | {{< var h2_holm >}} | Not supported: too few fee recipients |
| Specialists vs primary care | {{< var h3 >}} pp | {{< var h3_holm >}} | Not supported |
| First-year $100 or more vs under $100 | {{< var h4 >}} pp | {{< var h4_holm_fmt >}} | Gradient; higher-paid doctors are more selected |
| Paid brand's share (log-odds, matched) | {{< var h5 >}} pp | {{< var h5_holm >}} | Supported, pooled; rests on matching and on how hidden counts are treated |
| 30-day fills (matched, hidden cells at their cap) | {{< var h6 >}}% | {{< var h6_holm_fmt >}} | Volume rises, but much of it matches overall practice growth ({{< var matched_claims_growth >}}% in total claims); {{< var h6_min >}}% to {{< var h6_max >}}% depending on how hidden cells are bounded |
| Nurse practitioners and physician assistants | {{< var h7 >}} pp | {{< var h7_holm_fmt >}} | Supported, with the same targeting caveat; payments reported only from 2021, no matched version |

: Secondary hypotheses. Data: [secondary_family.csv](qa/secondary_family.csv). {tbl-colwidths="[30,13,13,44]"}
:::

Subgroup estimates by region, rural or urban setting and specialty, which inherit the same targeting caveat, are in the [results log](https://github.com/johnpospisil/pharma-payments-glp1/blob/main/docs/results.md) with the specialty payment chart.

## Falsification and robustness

::: {.table-scroll}
| Test | What would sink the finding | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-payment trend, ≥ 11 claims | Paid doctors already rising | **Fails**: steep rising trend for all three brands |
| Pre-payment trend, brand share | Share already rising | **Mixed**: passes for Trulicity unmatched (p = {{< var share_pre_trulicity >}}) but fails matched (p = {{< var share_pre_trulicity_matched >}}); drift for Ozempic; fails for Victoza; weak for Mounjaro |
| Hidden small counts, brand share | Gain is a suppression artefact | **Shrinks** to {{< var bound_trulicity >}} / {{< var bound_ozempic >}} / {{< var bound_mounjaro >}} pp under the least favourable bound (Trulicity / Ozempic / Mounjaro) |
| Statins (negative-control outcome) | Statins rise too | **Fails** for all three: {{< var statin_trulicity >}} / {{< var statin_victoza >}} / {{< var statin_ozempic >}} pp |
| Anticoagulant payments (negative-control exposure) | Unrelated payments predict GLP-1 prescribing as strongly | **Passes** the registered rule, but unrelated payments still predict {{< var nc_anticoag_ratio >}}% of the association with any GLP-1 prescribing |
| Inhaled-respiratory payments (second negative-control exposure) | Same | **Fails** ({{< var nc_inhaled_ratio >}}%); AstraZeneca and GSK also sell GLP-1s |
| Fake payment dates one or two years early | "Effects" before the real payment | **Passes** the registered rule (small relative to the estimate), though fake dates still give up to {{< var placebo_max >}} pp |
| Ozempic payment → Trulicity prescribing (placebo brand) | Competitor rises too | **Fails** in levels ({{< var placebo_brand_oz >}} pp), but Trulicity's *share* falls |
| HonestDiD sensitivity | Small violations of parallel trends erase it | Survives trend breaks up to {{< var honest_trulicity >}}× / {{< var honest_victoza >}}× / {{< var honest_ozempic >}}× the largest year-to-year pre-period change; if the pre-trend simply continued, about half remains |
| {{< var n_specs >}} alternative specifications | Effect depends on choices | Stays positive and above the 2-point threshold in all: {{< var sens_trulicity >}} / {{< var sens_victoza >}} / {{< var sens_ozempic >}} pp |

: Falsification and robustness for Trulicity / Victoza / Ozempic unless noted. The last two rows test how stable the ≥ 11-claims association is; they do not show that payments cause it. Fake dates can pass while trends rise because they are compared with not-yet-paid doctors on the same rising path. Data: [falsification.csv](qa/falsification.csv), [sensitivity.csv](qa/sensitivity.csv), [review_p24.json](qa/review_p24.json). {tbl-colwidths="[28,28,44]"}
:::

The failures mostly point the same way: paid doctors run larger and faster-growing practices. They undermine the volume result, which is why it is reported as targeting. They leave the direction of the brand-share result standing, but its size is small once the hidden counts are taken seriously.

## Limitations

- **Targeting is not ruled out, only partly removed.** Matching balances prior brand prescribing but not overall practice growth; matched paid doctors' practices grow even faster relative to their comparisons than unmatched ones, and the statin test fails even when matched on growth. Brand share removes practice size, but not earlier adoption of new brands, or visits timed to label changes (Victoza 2017, Ozempic and Trulicity 2020), formulary wins or the 2022–2024 shortages, which could raise a brand's share without the payment doing anything.
- **The share result is modest and model-dependent.** It is precise under the linear estimators but imprecise under the pre-registered log-odds form, where only Mounjaro is clear on its own, and it shrinks below the 2-point threshold under the least favourable treatment of hidden counts.
- **Annual data blur timing.** Payments arrive during the year, so the payment year is partly before and partly after.
- **Claims are not patients.** A claim is a pharmacy fill; dose-step fills for a newly started brand add claims without adding patients. Counting 30-day fills instead gives the same share result.
- **Who is studied.** Medicare Part D only (not commercial insurance or Medicaid); physicians first reached mostly by sponsored meals; nurse practitioners and physician assistants only from 2021. Medicare price negotiation for semaglutide (prices from 2027) and the 2025 kidney indication for Ozempic come after these data.
- **Spillovers.** Payments to one doctor may change colleagues' prescribing [@agha2022; @hyman2025]. Comparison doctors in practices where nobody was paid give *larger* estimates, consistent with spillovers biasing the main estimate down, though those practices also differ in other ways.

## Ethics: why no individual doctors appear

Open Payments names every recipient, and it would be easy to publish a league table. This project deliberately does not. A payment is legal, most are a sponsored meal worth tens of dollars, and a doctor who prescribes a paid brand may be prescribing well; a ranking would invite conclusions about individuals that aggregate data cannot support. Payment records are reported by companies and were not checked with the doctors. Every published figure and table aggregates at least 11 prescribers per cell, and cells are also withheld when one prescriber received more than half of the dollars, or when a hidden value could be worked out from the published totals. Code uses prescriber identifiers internally; nothing released contains them.

## Reproducibility

All data are public. The pipeline (Python 3.12, DuckDB; R only for cross-checking the estimators) rebuilds every number and figure from the raw federal files with one command, `make all`, in about two hours. Two independent rebuilds produce identical results. Every number in this article is read from the pipeline's QA outputs, never typed by hand, and a test fails if one is. Code, pre-registration, deviations and the QA report: [github.com/johnpospisil/pharma-payments-glp1](https://github.com/johnpospisil/pharma-payments-glp1).

**What is new here.** Earlier work, including the closest design [@carey2021], established that payments and prescribing go together, mostly from cross-sectional snapshots of older drugs. This project follows Medicare GLP-1 prescribers brand by brand over twelve years with estimators built for staggered timing, tests brand switching directly, and reports the negative controls and suppression bounds that cut against its own headline.
